title: Build Process
intro: Every project follows the same working loop. The table below defines each step; the project rows show how that loop shows up across math modeling, coding & trading, and engineering work.

steps.title: Question
steps.description: What problem is worth exploring, and what would a useful answer look like?

steps.title: Research
steps.description: Learn the theory, study existing work, identify assumptions, and decide what evidence is needed.

steps.title: Build
steps.description: Create a model, prototype, algorithm, or design that can make the question testable.

steps.title: Test
steps.description: Collect evidence, compare outputs, check assumptions, and look for failure modes.

steps.title: Improve
steps.description: Use the results to revise the model, design, or experiment—and document what changed.

projectWalkthroughs.title: FEM Quantum Harmonic Oscillator
cells: How accurately can finite element methods reproduce a quantum system with known analytical energy levels?
Reviewed the quantum harmonic oscillator, FEM theory, and linear vs. Hermite element tradeoffs.
Implemented spatial discretization, generalized eigenvalue formulation, and both linear and cubic Hermite assemblies.
Compared computed eigenvalues and wavefunctions against known analytical results across mesh sizes.
Adopted higher-order Hermite elements where fewer DOFs achieved substantially better accuracy.

projectWalkthroughs.title: HiMCM Graph Diffusion Model
cells: Which pollution interventions most effectively reduce exposure when effects propagate through a connected urban network?
Studied graph diffusion, environmental justice exposure, and network structure in Chelsea and Everett, MA.
Built a 486-node, 20,303-edge network with steady-state diffusion and four policy scenarios.
Ranked interventions (anti-idling near schools, electric freight, low-emission zones, industrial reduction) with sensitivity analysis.
Interpreted rankings with explicit assumptions about propagation, equity tradeoffs, and model limits.

projectWalkthroughs.title: HiMCM Evacuation Sweep Optimization
cells: What order should firefighters search rooms in, where should they enter, and how many firefighters are actually useful when the building is changing around them?
We started with the six-room office from the problem and looked into graph routing, how hazards change travel time, and what information firefighters would realistically have during a sweep.

We built three versions, first a static weighted graph, then one with changing fire and smoke costs, and finally one that could deal with uncertain information and reassign firefighters while the sweep was happening.
We tested the models on the original layout, a two-floor building, and a 24-room building spread across three floors, while requiring every room to be checked twice.

The later models avoided more dangerous routes and helped us find where extra firefighters stopped making much of a difference, but we also wrote about the limits of using simulated hazards instead of data from real fires.

projectWalkthroughs.title: Penny Phase-Out Diffusion Model
cells: How will penny acceptance diffuse across urban, suburban, and rural regions—and what are the economic tradeoffs of cash rounding?
Reviewed diffusion processes, regional population density, and business cash-handling behavior.
Formulated density-dependent nonlinear differential equations with regional adoption rates and rounding analysis.
Projected adoption curves by region and identified the price threshold where rounding up beats rounding down.
Documented how spatial heterogeneity changes the timeline of an apparently simple policy transition.

projectWalkthroughs.title: AV & Emissions Policy Model (Boston)
cells: Which autonomous-vehicle policy levers most cost-effectively reduce pollution and congestion without triggering rebound effects?
Studied fleet adoption dynamics, ZIP-code traffic flow, PM2.5 dispersion, and Boston exposure corridors.
Coupled logistic adoption, cell transmission traffic, and convection–diffusion dispersion models across 11 scenarios.
Compared pollution reduction per dollar and VMT rebound risk across rebates, infrastructure, and supply-side incentives.
Prioritized equity-focused recommendations for high-exposure ZIP codes 02126, 02131, and 02127.

projectWalkthroughs.title: Etosha Wildlife Protection Model
cells: Where should limited ranger, drone, camera, and sensor resources go to reduce poaching, wildfire, and habitat pressure?
Mapped Etosha ecology, five guilds, seasonal vulnerability, and operational capacity constraints.
Built a 940-cell spatial grid with wet/dry seasonality and optimization for patrols, drones, cameras, and acoustic sensors.
Ran scenario forecasts and sensitivity analyses on protection capacity and risk assumptions.
Produced reproducible risk maps and operational placement recommendations under funding limits.

projectWalkthroughs.title: Etosha Rhino Anti-Poaching Patrol Routing
cells: Given limited vehicles and ranger-hours, where should Etosha patrols drive to cover rhino poaching risk?
Combined Model-1 risk and habitat surfaces with Etosha’s real OpenStreetMap road network and five ranger camps.
Formulated a multi-depot team orienteering problem and solved routes with Google OR-Tools guided local search.
Benchmarked against greedy, risk-only, habitat-only, and random baselines; stress-tested under risk-map noise.
Five eight-hour patrols covered ~26% of risk-reward and 70–80% of top-priority cells, with strongest marginal value in the west.

projectWalkthroughs.title: M3C Sports Gambling Model
cells: How do structural expected losses, financial vulnerability, and social contagion interact to spread harmful gambling over time?
Analyzed ~3M demographic records, betting theory, stochastic processes, and network contagion literature.
Built regression and TabNet income models, Monte Carlo wealth simulation, and a network contagion layer.
Projected 5-, 15-, and 30-year harm horizons and quantified structural losses from house edge.
Framed prevention-focused policy recommendations from compounding disadvantage—not isolated decisions.

projectWalkthroughs.title: ARTICULATE
cells: How can speech technology support clearer communication for people with atypical speech—without changing what they mean to say?
Studied Whisper, Flan-T5, accessibility requirements, and UX needs for users, caregivers, and speech-language pathologists.
Built a browser app with speech recognition, grammar repair, TTS playback, waveform feedback, and API fallbacks.
Evaluated transcription quality, latency, and meaning preservation in real-time communication workflows.
Refined model loading, failure handling, and interface design with accessibility as a core constraint—not an add-on.

projectWalkthroughs.title: IMC Prosperity Trading
cells: How can a five-person team coordinate trading strategies to manage risk and capture opportunity in dynamic simulated markets?
Studied market microstructure, backtesting methods, and team strategy coordination under competition constraints.
Developed Python algorithms for pattern detection, price-inefficiency identification, and risk-managed decision rules.
Iteratively backtested strategies in simulation and compared performance across changing market conditions.
Refined team communication and strategy rules from results—top 25% worldwide with ~73,000 simulated tokens.

projectWalkthroughs.title: STATERA (GVS Glasses)
cells: Most devices only react once a fall has started, could we detect the problem early enough to do something before the person fell?
We looked into different ways of affecting balance and I found galvanic vestibular stimulation, then we researched how GVS, IMUs, and the vestibular system worked.
We built the prototype with three IMUs, an ESP32, electrodes, a custom PCB that I designed in EasyEDA, and a 3D-printed glasses frame.
We ran 50 controlled trials and checked both whether the system recognized a balance event and whether the participant detected the stimulation.
We kept changing the electronics, PCB, frame, and testing process until the system reached 88% classification accuracy, with detectable stimulation in every active trial.

projectWalkthroughs.title: Flo-Wrist
cells: How can a low-cost wearable help users adopt healthier wrist posture before cumulative strain becomes injury?
Defined risky wrist orientations, ergonomic criteria, and validation positions (30°, 45°, 60°).
Built brace prototype with IMUs, sensor fusion, tactile/visual alerts, and exercise prompts.
Collected validation data against physical measurements and ergonomic test criteria.
Tightened calibration, feedback thresholds, and reporting from fit between model and measured wrist angles.

projectWalkthroughs.title: FRC Team 190
cells: How can a competition team iterate subsystem designs quickly while supporting broader FIRST community outreach?
Reviewed mechanism requirements, Onshape CAD workflows, and FLL mentorship needs.
Prototyped and CAD-designed robot subsystems; built FLL kits and practice mats; contributed to Impact and social media teams.
Gathered teammate feedback through fabrication cycles and competition-season testing.
Revised designs and outreach materials from real build feedback and community events.

projectWalkthroughs.title: FRC Team 467
cells: What mechanical designs fit the constraints of a team robotics environment and real fabrication limits?
Reviewed mechanism requirements, Onshape workflows, and knee mill, CNC, and lathe capabilities.
Designed and documented CAD assemblies; prototyped and machined competition components.
Assembled, tested mechanisms, and gathered feedback from iteration cycles.
Revised designs based on fabrication limits, testing results, and team input—FIRST Leadership Award recipient.
